query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a predominantly fcc matrix, degradation at elevated temperatures is governed by grain boundary–mediated diffusion of reactive elements (primarily Al, Cr, and Ti). In oxidizing atmospheres, this diffusion promotes the selective formation of a thin, continuous protective oxide (Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) along the grain boundaries that passivates further oxidation, whereas in reducing atmospheres the absence of sufficient oxygen prevents stable scale formation, leading instead to localized internal oxidation and grain-boundary weakening due to Ti segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured alloy with a nanocrystalline fcc matrix and a uniform distribution of alloying elements.
generation.intervention: Controlled exposure of the alloy to elevated temperatures in either oxidizing or reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., around or above 900°C) with defined environments: one set in an oxygen-rich (oxidizing) atmosphere and the other in an oxygen-lean or hydrogen-rich (reducing) atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries acting as fast diffusion paths for reactive elements, serving as nucleation sites for oxide scale formation (or for internal oxidation in low-oxygen conditions).
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, reactive elements diffuse preferentially along grain boundaries. In an oxidizing environment, these elements react with the available oxygen to form a coherent, adherent oxide layer that retards further degradation. In contrast, under reducing conditions, the lack of oxygen inhibits stable scale formation, leading to localized depletion of elements (especially Ti) and the nucleation of internal oxide precipitates that compromise grain-boundary integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will form a thin, continuous protective oxide scale (evidenced by uniform grain boundary oxidation and minimal internal oxidation) that slows further degradation, while those in reducing conditions will exhibit discontinuous or absent surface oxides with localized internal oxidation along grain boundaries, leading to accelerated degradation and compromised mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy state, characterized by a uniform nanocrystalline fcc matrix with homogenous elemental distribution and no pre-existing oxidation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under temperatures high enough (e.g., ≥900°C) to activate significant grain-boundary diffusion and under gas compositions where the oxygen partial pressure is either sufficiently high to induce continuous oxide scale formation or low enough (in reducing conditions) to prevent it.
generation.uncertainty: The exact diffusion kinetics of the reactive elements and the quantitative differences in oxide layer thickness, as well as the possible influence of any secondary phases that might form during exposure, remain uncertain and require further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical AM HEA samples and subject them to isothermal exposure at an elevated temperature (e.g., 950°C) for several time intervals. One set is exposed to an oxidizing atmosphere (high O2 partial pressure) and the other to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2-rich environment). Analyze the samples using SEM and TEM for microstructural changes, perform surface analysis (XPS/EDS) to characterize oxide scale formation and elemental segregation along grain boundaries, and evaluate mechanical properties (e.g., microhardness testing).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity at grain boundaries
Extent and distribution of internal oxidation (especially Ti-rich oxides)
Mechanical integrity indicators such as microhardness or fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing exposures result in similar oxide scale formation and degradation patterns (i.e., no significant difference in grain-boundary oxidation or internal oxidation features) or if grain-boundary diffusion/segregation of reactive elements is not observed, then the hypothesis would be rejected.

Question: How do mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the phase evolution, microstructure refinement, and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys?. System: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions of Cobalt, Chromium, Iron, Nickel, and Titanium). Processing: Mechanical alloying using a planetary ball mill (QM-1SP4) at 400 rpm for 1–6 hours under argon atmosphere, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) in a vacuum at 900–1000 °C for 10 minutes with a heating rate of 50 °C/min. Test conditions: Vickers hardness testing at 0.05 kN load with 15 s dwell time; compressive strength tests at a displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min (strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹); XRD analysis with Cu-Kα radiation (2θ range 20°–80°); SEM and TEM for microstructural analysis.
